posts.body_html:
The Iris family seems to naturally occur throughout the world and comes in all sorts of different shapes and sizes. Fortunately for us, due to the extreme variance and adaptability of the genus Iris, much like the genus Lilium, there are some species of Iris that tolerate bog conditions and are outstanding companion plants to carnivorous plants.

Normally, Irises "don't do it for me" in general (with a few exceptions because there are some really beautiful bearded irises out there ). However, some populations of Iris verna, especially this one I acquired that originated from Onslow Co, NC, are jaw droppers! The incredible contrasting neon blue and orange color, as well as a dense, profusion of blooms on well established plants, makes this plant a worthy endeavor! Leaves are short and the plants form very compact tufts over time. Well, we haven't gotten to the point of producing massive numbers blooms that fill the pot, but I've only had the plant fora full season and some change now, so hopefully in time it'll get there.

So what is the trick to growing Iris verna? There's still much to be learned, but it does seem like the key is to grow them somewhat as though it were a carnivorous plant. Much like Lilium catesbaei, this Iris is nutrient sensitive and needs to be grown like a Sarracenia, except it can tolerate slightly higher concentrations of salt in the soil and does not like to sit in water. Here's how I grow them:
1)100% peat moss, kept moist at all times all year round. Keep damp but not water logged during the winter dormancy period. During the grow season, It can sit in water for a day or two, seems to sulk if you keep it waterlogged.
2) Fertilize with 1/4 strength maxsea 1-2x per month only during the grow season (probably 1x a month to be on the safe side). Be careful! I have personally burned the plant (see brown leaves pictured below), so maybe try 1/5 strength first.
3) grow in full sun.
4) Plant goes dormant-ish during the winter, and appears to need a cool winter dormancy to bloom.


Here's some photos of Iris verna from Onslow Co, NC. I just love how short and miniature these plants are! The flowers are barely above ground!!! photos taken late March 2018. It's pretty difficult to caputure the neon blue colors you see in person, but some of these photos come pretty close:



Some spent flowers pictured here as well. Nice thing is they don't all seem to bloom at once, so this prolongs the show to several weeks:



Ellie's reaction when she saw this flower:





Check out that orange flare....yup, they tend to wear a lot of flare, as the flower is trying to express itself (joke from Office Space in case you were wondering):






The flowers are very mildly fragrant, but you need "20/20" smell to detect it. There's still a lot to learn about this species, and I'll update this thread as more information is ascertained.

posts.body_html:
Thanks guys! What's funny is immediately after seeing this bloom, I scoured the internet to see if I could purchase another clone, but not surprisingly, can't find it anywhere! Only one place offers a similar Iris verna, but the plant offered seems a bit different than the one in this thread (ie. not as colorful), and is perhaps a different sub species. I'm starting to suspect that many of the nurseries may not completely understand how to grow this plant because they probably aren't growing it like a carnivorous plant! In my eyes, this plant like Lilium catesbaei awesome, and there's a ginormous appetite from the general public for that plant.

A lot of the websites suggest growing Iris verna in part shade, and maybe that's true for some subspecies or even particular genotypes, but the one I have is thriving in full sun, so I'm going to recommend that for the time being. The plant will hopefully get pretty massive this summer and if all goes to plan, it will be divided probably early fall.



During the cool winter dormancy period, I noticed there's a lot of underground activity (ie. new growth points emerging in various directions). The decrease in photoperiod during the fall also might trigger the formation of flower buds on plants that are at reproductive maturity.

Okay Mike meizzwang, you got me going in an internet "do-loop" about Iris verna.  Apparently it is native to Ohio, but rather uncommon and restricted to the southern hills.  Curiously, in the words of at least one blogger, "Most iris species are associated with wet-moist soiled situations but the vernal iris is a high and dry plant that prefers the xeric, sun-drenched ridge tops and rocky outcrops of extreme southern Ohio." link  Hmmmm, quite different and wondering if its due to it being a northern end of its geographic range, or if the one in Ohio is a slightly different subspecies.  Now I'm on a quest to find a few sources of it and try in my own garden.

Also, I now have a further reason to get rid of the Iris pseudacorus, because I found in midst of my googling that it is listed as "well established invasive" in Ohio!  Crap, like a really need an additional invasive on my property after the wintercreeper, honeysuckle, lesser celandine....

It's not unheard of for a dry land/xeric plants to thrive in an acid bog setting. Viola pedata typically grows in crazy dry, impoverished soils. I had a heck of a time propagating it until I went to a wild site and did some soil testing: pH 4 and conductivity of 50mS/cm!

When I transferred them all to peat/sand, they did great. Then, stray seeds started popping up amongst the Sarracenia.

So, some of these xerophiles colonize acidic areas because they can tolerate the soil chemistry, and are adaptable in regards to moisture. I. verna, being a pine/oak woodlander, requires acidic soil. I've not seen it here, in VA, though it's native. I. cristata is more common; I've got patches in my yard of blue and white-flowered selections.

Wish I could find a good source for Iris chrysographes. I have some on order from White Flower Farm…we'll see.

They are nice but you should see Japanese irises Ensata, those are well adapted to growing in bog as long as it does not freeze, and they are really jaw dropper, with flowers the size of a plate. I keep mine in tray of water, just like the sarracenias and they do love full sun and warm temperature, just like the sarracenias. The only difference is that they love a rich medium with manure, so they don't really go well with sarracenias, but beside that, they grow in the same conditions.

They bloom in June, and each time they do, I spend hours just looking at them. They are far from miniature though, they can grow up to 3 feet high.

I own a good collection of these irises and they are just amazing, here from ensata.com
